title: IF GOD ALREADY KNOWS EVERYTHING, WHY DOES HE STILL ASK YOU TO PRAY?
paragraphs: IF GOD ALREADY KNOWS EVERYTHING, WHY DOES HE STILL ASK YOU TO PRAY?
The heartbreaking truth about unanswered prayers, the silence of heaven, and the Father who knows what you need before you ever find the strength to ask.
What if I told you that the prayer you almost didn't pray last night mattered more than you realized?
The one you whispered while everyone else was sleeping.
The one that barely made it past your trembling lips.
The one where you couldn't even finish the sentence because the tears came first.
And perhaps the most painful part wasn't that God hadn't answered.
It was the question you were almost afraid to ask.
"Lord, if You already know everything I'm going through, why do I have to keep telling You?"
You know the bills are overdue.
You know my marriage is struggling.
You know my child is drifting away from You.
You know what the doctor said.
You know the temptation I keep fighting, the sin I keep confessing, the fear I hide behind my smile.
You know how exhausted I am.
You know how many times I've prayed about the same thing.
So why, Lord?
Why must I keep asking a God who already knows?
And why does heaven sometimes seem so painfully quiet?
If you've ever wrestled with those questions, don't turn away from this conversation.
Because Jesus addressed something extraordinary about prayer that many believers have read a hundred times without recognizing its significance.
And once you understand it, you may never approach the throne of grace quite the same way again.
Jesus said:
"For your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." — Matthew 6:8, KJV
Read that again.
Before you ask.
Not after you explain everything.
Not after you've prayed for three hours.
Not after you've found the perfect words.
Before.
Jesus didn't say the Father discovers your needs when you pray.
He said your Father already knows.
And yet, only a few verses later, Jesus taught His disciples to pray.
"Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name." (Matthew 6:9, KJV)
Do you see the beautiful tension?
The same Jesus who declared that the Father already knows our needs also commanded us to bring those needs before Him.
That means prayer cannot simply be about giving God information.
Something deeper is happening.
Something far more personal.
And to understand it, we need to go back to the words Jesus actually used.
In the Greek text of Matthew 6:8, we find this remarkable statement:
οἶδεν γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὧν χρείαν ἔχετε πρὸ τοῦ ὑμᾶς αἰτῆσαι αὐτόν.
Oiden gar ho patēr hymōn hōn chreian echete pro tou hymas aitēsai auton.
A faithful translation is:
"For your Father knows what you need before you ask Him."
Notice the word οἶδεν (oiden).
It means "knows."
Jesus is not describing a Father who needs to be informed, persuaded that suffering exists, or awakened to a crisis.
He is describing a Father who already possesses knowledge of His children's needs.
And notice something else.
Jesus doesn't merely say "God knows."
He says ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν (ho patēr hymōn).
"Your Father."
Those two words change the emotional center of the entire passage.
Jesus is teaching His disciples to approach God not as strangers trying to obtain an audience with a distant ruler, but as children approaching their heavenly Father.
The difference is enormous.
Imagine a little boy waking up in the middle of the night.
He's frightened.
Thunder is shaking the windows.
His father already knows there's a storm outside.
His father already knows the child is afraid of thunder.
He may even hear the little footsteps coming down the hallway.
But when the boy reaches his father's room and whispers, "Daddy, I'm scared," does the father respond:
"I already know that. Why are you telling me?"
No.
A loving father welcomes his child.
Not because he needed information about the storm.
But because the child needed the comfort of his father's presence.
And while every earthly father is imperfect, Jesus tells us that our heavenly Father is greater in goodness than even the most loving human parent (Matthew 7:9–11).
Prayer is not informing an ignorant God. It is approaching a knowing Father.
But that raises another question.
If God knows our needs, why doesn't He simply give us everything without our asking?
Why would He make prayer part of the process at all?
The answer begins with something many of us have painfully misunderstood.
God did not create us merely to receive things from Him.
He created human beings for fellowship with Himself.
Sin shattered that fellowship.
And the Gospel is the astonishing announcement that Jesus Christ came to reconcile sinners to God.
Not merely to improve our circumstances.
Not merely to make our lives easier.
But to bring us back to the Father.
"For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God." (1 Peter 3:18, KJV)
Did you catch the purpose?
That He might bring us to God.
Not simply bring us blessings.
Bring us to God Himself.
This is why prayer is so much more than a spiritual request form.
Through Christ, we are invited into communion with the God who made us.
The God who knows us.
The God before whom nothing is hidden.
The God who nevertheless welcomes His redeemed children to draw near.
And perhaps this is where the truth begins to hurt a little.
Because many of us have treated prayer like an emergency telephone.
We call when the money runs out.
We call when someone gets sick.
We call when the relationship falls apart.
We call when our carefully constructed plans collapse.
And there is nothing wrong with crying out to God in an emergency. Scripture repeatedly invites us to do exactly that.
But what happens when the emergency passes?
When the test results improve?
When the job finally comes?
When the relationship is restored?
Do we still seek His face?
Or do we quietly put the phone down until the next disaster?
That question isn't meant to shame the wounded.
It's meant to expose something we all need to examine.
Have we been seeking the Father's heart, or only His hand?
Because the greatest gift of prayer is not always the answer we receive.
Sometimes it is the deeper knowledge of God we gain while waiting.
And that brings us to one of the most misunderstood passages in the Bible.
Jesus said:
"Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." (Matthew 7:7, KJV)
The Greek verbs are striking.
αἰτεῖτε (aiteite) — ask.
ζητεῖτε (zēteite) — seek.
κρούετε (krouete) — knock.
These are present-tense imperatives. In this context, they encourage an ongoing posture of asking, seeking, and knocking.
Not a single desperate moment followed by permanent silence.
A continuing life of dependence upon God.
But we must be careful.
Jesus is not promising that every requested outcome will arrive exactly as we imagine.
He immediately explains that our heavenly Father gives what is good to His children (Matthew 7:9–11).
And sometimes what we desperately want is not what our Father, in His wisdom, knows is best.
That truth can be difficult to hear.
Especially when the thing you are asking for isn't selfish.
You're not asking for luxury.
You're asking for your mother to survive.
You're asking for your husband to come home.
You're asking for your daughter to return to Christ.
You're asking for the pain to stop.
And someone tells you, "Just pray harder."
As though the problem must be that you haven't cried enough.
Believed enough.
Fastened enough faith onto the outcome.
But the Bible gives us a very different picture.
There was a man who loved Jesus deeply.
A man who preached the Gospel, suffered for Christ, and experienced extraordinary revelations.
His name was Paul.
And Paul had a problem he begged God to remove.
He called it a thorn in the flesh.
Scripture does not identify precisely what the thorn was, and we should not pretend to know.
But we do know this.
It tormented him.
And he prayed about it.
Not casually.
Not indifferently.
Three times, Paul pleaded with the Lord that it might depart from him.
And God's answer was not the removal Paul requested.
Instead, the Lord said:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Imagine that.
The apostle Paul prayed.
God heard.
And the thorn remained.
Was Paul lacking faith?
Was he spiritually immature?
Had he failed to discover some secret formula for answered prayer?
No.
The Lord was teaching him to depend upon divine grace in the very place where human strength was failing.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that tonight.
An unanswered request is not proof that you are an unloved child.
Your continued struggle does not automatically mean your prayers are defective.
Your tears do not mean God has abandoned you.
Sometimes He removes the thorn.
Sometimes He sustains His children through it.
And sometimes, in ways we cannot yet understand, He calls us to trust Him without revealing why the pain remains.
That is not an easy answer.
It is not supposed to be.
Christian faith does not require us to pretend that suffering is painless.
The Psalms are filled with cries of bewilderment, grief, and longing.
"How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" (Psalm 13:1, KJV)
That question came from David.
A man after God's own heart.
And God preserved his anguished words in Scripture.
Think about that.
The Bible does not erase the prayers of people who struggled to understand God's silence.
It gives those prayers a voice.
So if you've been afraid to tell God how much you're hurting, remember this:
He already knows.
And you can bring your sorrow before Him without pretending to be stronger than you are.
But there is an even deeper mystery.
One that takes us from the suffering of Paul to a dark garden outside Jerusalem.
Gethsemane.
The night before the crucifixion.
Jesus knew what was coming.
He knew betrayal was near.
He knew the cross awaited Him.
He knew the terrible suffering He would endure as He gave His life for sinners.
And yet He prayed.
Matthew tells us that Jesus fell on His face and said:
"O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." (Matthew 26:39, KJV)
Stop here for a moment.
If knowing the Father's will made prayer unnecessary, why did Jesus pray in Gethsemane?
The eternal Son, who lived in perfect fellowship with the Father, prayed in the hour of His deepest anguish.
Not because the Father lacked knowledge.
Not because the Son lacked obedience.
But in the reality of His human suffering, Jesus expressed His anguish and submitted Himself to the Father's will.
He did not hide His distress.
He did not pretend the cup was easy.
He brought the horror of what lay ahead before His Father.
And He surrendered.
"Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."
Those words should forever change the way we understand prayer.
Because prayer is not a technique for forcing heaven to obey earth.
It is one of the ways God's children learn to entrust themselves to the Father.
And Jesus demonstrated that trust perfectly.
The cup was not taken away.
The cross still came.
But the cross was not evidence that the Father had lost control.
It was central to God's saving purpose.
At Calvary, the sinless Christ bore our sins, suffering in the place of sinners.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The greatest act of redemption in history came through suffering that was not removed.
Now, be careful with that truth.
It does not mean every tragedy in your life will produce a visible triumph in this world.
It does not mean you can look at another person's suffering and confidently explain God's hidden reasons.
We cannot.
But the death and resurrection of Jesus give believers a reason to trust the goodness of God even when His purposes remain beyond our understanding.
Because at the cross, God demonstrated His love not by avoiding suffering, but by giving His Son for our salvation.
"He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?" (Romans 8:32, KJV)
In context, Paul is assuring believers of God's faithful love and ultimate saving purpose in Christ, not guaranteeing an easy life or every earthly possession.
The cross tells us that God's love is real.
The resurrection tells us that death does not have the final word.
And prayer draws us back to the One in whom that hope is found.
But perhaps you're still thinking:
"If God has already planned what will happen, can my prayers actually make any difference?"
That question deserves more than a comforting slogan.
The Bible teaches both that God is sovereign and that human prayer genuinely matters.
James writes:
And James also says:
"The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." (James 5:16, KJV)
He then points to Elijah, whose prayers were connected with the withholding and return of rain (James 5:17–18).
James is not presenting prayer as an illusion.
He is teaching that prayer is meaningful and effective.
How does this fit with God's complete knowledge and sovereign purposes?
Christians have expressed different understandings of the precise relationship between divine sovereignty and human freedom.
But Scripture does not ask us to choose between a God who knows and a people who pray.
It teaches both.
God knows what will happen.
And He commands us to pray.
He is able to accomplish His purposes through the very prayers He calls His people to offer.
In other words, God's foreknowledge does not make prayer meaningless.
The God who knows the outcome also knows the prayers that will be offered along the way.
Think of the early church.
Peter was imprisoned.
Herod had already killed James, the brother of John.
The situation was terrifying.
But Acts 12:5 tells us:
"Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him."
The church prayed.
And God sent an angel to deliver Peter.
It was an extraordinary intervention.
But notice something important.
Earlier in the same chapter, James had been killed.
The church did not live in a world where every faithful servant escaped suffering.
God delivered Peter.
James died.
Both were servants of Christ.
And the different outcomes do not permit us to conclude that one was loved more or prayed for more faithfully.
This is where our theology of prayer must grow beyond simple formulas.
God is not a machine.
Prayer is not a payment.
Faith is not a lever that guarantees the result we desire.
Our heavenly Father is wise, sovereign, holy, and good.
And He has invited us to pray because our prayers truly matter within His providential care.
Yet there is another reason prayer matters that is easy to overlook.
Prayer reveals what is happening inside us.
Not to inform God.
To bring us honestly before Him.
Consider David's prayer in Psalm 139.
First, he acknowledges that God knows him completely.
"O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me." (Psalm 139:1, KJV)
Later, he confesses:
"For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether." (Psalm 139:4, KJV)
God knows David's thoughts.
God knows his words before they are spoken.
And yet, near the end of the psalm, David prays:
"Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." (Psalm 139:23, KJV)
Wait.
Didn't David just say God already knows?
Yes.
And that's precisely the point.
David is not asking God to acquire missing information.
He is inviting God's searching work into the depths of his life.
He wants his heart examined.
His anxious thoughts exposed.
His sinful ways revealed.
His steps directed in the everlasting way.
That is one of the most transformative dimensions of prayer.
Sometimes we enter prayer determined to change our circumstances.
And through God's Word and the work of His Spirit, we discover that our hearts also need changing.
We begin by praying, "Lord, change that person."
And we find ourselves convicted about our own bitterness.
We begin by praying, "Lord, give me more."
And we discover that envy has been quietly ruling our hearts.
We begin by praying, "Lord, make them apologize."
And we realize that we, too, have wounds to acknowledge and sins to confess.
Not every hardship is caused by personal sin.
And we must never assume that suffering itself proves someone is spiritually compromised.
But prayer, joined with Scripture and honest repentance, creates space for the Spirit to expose what we would rather conceal.
And sometimes the hardest prayer isn't:
"Lord, give me what I want."
It's:
"Lord, show me what I don't want to see about myself."
That's where transformation begins.
Not in pretending to be righteous.
But in bringing our actual hearts before a holy and merciful God.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtakingly personal.
Because the God who knows everything about you also knows the things you hope nobody ever discovers.
The pride.
The lust.
The resentment.
The secret dishonesty.
The compromises you rationalized.
The promises you made and broke.
The prayers you stopped praying because you were ashamed to approach Him again.
You may have fooled the people around you.
You may have perfected the language of Christianity.
You may know exactly when to say "Amen," when to raise your hands, and how to look spiritually strong.
But God knows.
He knows the truth behind the carefully maintained image.
And that knowledge can be terrifying.
Unless you understand what Jesus came to do.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that God finally discovered you were worth saving.
It is the announcement that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
Jesus did not go to the cross because our sins were hidden from Him.
He went to the cross to save sinners.
And the resurrection declares that His saving work is victorious.
Consider Peter.
He had confidently promised loyalty.
He had insisted that even if others abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
But when fear came, Peter denied his Lord.
Three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
Can you imagine that moment?
The crushing realization.
The shame.
The memory of every boast.
The knowledge that the One he loved had seen his failure.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The man who denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of Jesus' restoring grace.
And perhaps that is the message somebody needs more than anything else today.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because you failed.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because your prayer life collapsed.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because you made promises you didn't keep.
But grace does not mean sin is harmless.
It means there is a Savior who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His blood.
"Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out." (Acts 3:19, KJV)
The invitation is not to remain comfortably hidden.
It is to come into the light.
Confess.
Turn from sin.
Trust Jesus Christ.
And discover that the Savior who knows the worst about you is mighty to save.
This is the heartbeat of everything we proclaim at Gospel Warrior.
Not because our past never happened.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ truly forgives, reconciles, restores, and transforms those who come to Him in faith.
And when you understand that, prayer stops being a performance.
It becomes the cry of a redeemed sinner who knows where mercy can be found.
There is a beautiful word in the New Testament that helps us understand this privilege.
παρρησία (parrēsia).
It carries the sense of boldness, confidence, or freedom of speech.
Hebrews 4:16 says:
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."
The word translated "boldly" is connected to this idea of confident approach.
But notice where the confidence comes from.
The preceding verses point us to Jesus Christ, our great High Priest.
He sympathizes with our weaknesses.
He was tempted, yet without sin.
And because of Him, believers may approach God's throne.
Not arrogantly.
Not demanding.
Not because we have earned the right.
But confidently, through Christ.
The throne is still a throne.
God is still holy.
Yet for those who belong to Jesus, it is a throne of grace.
Think about that.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect emotional state before approaching Him.
You do not need to impress Him with religious vocabulary.
You do not need to hide your weakness.
You come through Jesus.
And when you don't even know what to say, Scripture gives us another extraordinary comfort.
Romans 8:26 tells us:
"Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered."
There are moments when suffering leaves us without words.
Moments when grief is so heavy that sentences feel impossible.
Moments when the only thing we can manage is a broken whisper.
"Jesus, help me."
And the believer is not abandoned in that weakness.
The Holy Spirit helps us.
Christ Himself also intercedes for His people (Romans 8:34).
Your hope does not rest on the elegance of your prayers.
It rests on the saving work of Jesus Christ and the faithful ministry of God.
That doesn't mean prayer requires no discipline.
Jesus taught His followers to pray.
Paul instructed believers to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17).
Prayer is a privilege and a responsibility.
But it is not a competition to see who can sound most spiritual.
It is communion with God through Christ.
And maybe that's why the shortest sincere prayer can be more honest than an hour of impressive religious speech.
Remember the tax collector in Luke 18?
He stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He struck his chest and prayed:
"God be merciful to me a sinner." (Luke 18:13, KJV)
No elaborate speech.
No attempt to impress the crowd.
Just a sinner pleading for mercy.
And Jesus said that man went home justified rather than the self-righteous Pharisee who boasted of his religious achievements.
Because God is not impressed by the performance of righteousness.
He calls us to humility, repentance, and faith.
So perhaps tonight your prayer doesn't need to begin with a list of demands.
Perhaps it needs to begin with the truth.
"Father, I'm tired."
"Father, I've been angry."
"Father, I don't understand why this is happening."
"Father, I have sinned."
"Father, I want to trust You, but I'm struggling."
"Father, please teach me to pray again."
And if you've never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, don't confuse religious activity with salvation.
Prayer itself does not purchase forgiveness.
A donation cannot purchase forgiveness.
Church attendance cannot purchase forgiveness.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is where the deepest restoration begins.
Not in getting every circumstance you wanted.
But in being reconciled to the God you were created to know.
And now, perhaps, we can return to the question that brought us here.
If God already knows everything, why does He tell us to pray?
Because He is our Father, not merely the supplier of our needs.
Because through Christ, we are invited to draw near.
Because He has ordained prayer as a meaningful part of our lives of faith.
Because prayer expresses dependence, worship, confession, thanksgiving, and trust.
Because in prayer we bring our requests before Him and learn to submit ourselves to His wisdom.
Because we are weak, and we need His grace.
Because our relationship with God was never meant to be reduced to what we could obtain from Him.
And because sometimes, while we are asking God to change what is happening around us, He is working through His Word and Spirit to change what is happening within us.
But please don't misunderstand.
Prayer is not always emotionally beautiful.
Sometimes it is exhausting.
Sometimes it is repetitive.
Sometimes you pray with confidence.
Sometimes you pray while trembling.
Sometimes you rejoice.
Sometimes you lament.
And sometimes you wait far longer than you ever imagined.
The Bible does not promise that every faithful Christian will live to see every earthly longing fulfilled.
But it does promise that those who belong to Christ are not separated from His love by tribulation, distress, persecution, or even death (Romans 8:35–39).
And it points us toward the day when God will wipe away every tear from His people's eyes (Revelation 21:4).
Until that day, we pray.
Not because God has forgotten.
Not because He is uninformed.
Not because we can manipulate His will.
We pray because Jesus has opened the way to the Father.
And we need Him.
Every single day.
Perhaps there is someone on your Facebook feed who is silently losing the strength to pray.
Someone who still attends church but feels spiritually empty.
Someone who has buried a loved one.
Someone whose marriage is breaking.
Someone who is ashamed to return to God after falling into the same sin again.
Someone who has begun to wonder whether heaven is listening.
Not merely to increase its reach.
But because one person may read it on the very night they were about to give up praying.
Let this be more than another article that appears on a screen and disappears into yesterday's feed.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read Matthew 6 again.
Read Gethsemane.
Read Romans 8.
Read the Psalms when your own words fail.
And please, don't leave this conversation without allowing yourself a moment of spiritual honesty.
You don't have to explain every detail publicly.
God knows the burden.
And fellow believers can stand with you in prayer.
Not every struggle needs to be disclosed online. Some burdens are best shared privately with a trusted pastor, mature Christian, or caring friend.
But none of us was meant to live the Christian life in isolation.
We need Scripture.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need encouragement and correction.
We need fellow believers who will remind us of the Gospel when our hearts are overwhelmed.
And that is why the mission of Gospel Warrior matters.
Not because Gospel Warrior can replace your local church.
Not because a digital ministry can replace pastoral care, Christian fellowship, or your personal time with God.
But biblical encouragement can reach people in places where a church conversation may not yet have reached them.
A weary parent scrolling after midnight.
A worker sitting alone during a break.
A young believer confused by false teaching.
A person who hasn't opened a Bible in years.
A sinner who thinks Jesus could never forgive what they've done.
And I want to invite you to consider something prayerfully.
Not out of guilt.
It doesn't.
We are saved by grace, not by financial support.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support faithful Gospel ministry.
Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14).
He also taught that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is not a mandatory biblical tithe, and it should not replace the giving and commitments you have prayerfully made elsewhere.
It is an opportunity to partner in a mission.
To help keep biblical teaching accessible.
To help sustain the work of writing, developing, and distributing resources.
To help us continue reaching people who need to hear about repentance, forgiveness, grace, and new life in Christ.
You are no less valued, no less welcome, and no less loved by God.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
These are simply tangible ways to say thank you.
The heart of this invitation remains discipleship and Gospel ministry.
We want people to be nourished by biblical truth, strengthened in faith, and continually pointed toward the Savior.
And if you decide to support, let your reason be love for Christ and a sincere desire to help His Gospel be proclaimed—not fear that God will withhold blessings if you don't.
It is to make Jesus Christ known.
To proclaim His Word faithfully.
To call sinners to repentance.
To encourage the brokenhearted.
To strengthen believers in truth.
And to remind the world that no human scandal is greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, I want you to imagine one final scene.
A person kneeling beside a bed.
The room is dark.
The house is silent.
Nothing about the circumstances has changed.
The medical report is still there.
The unpaid bill is still on the table.
The prodigal child is still far from home.
The unanswered question still hurts.
And the person whispers:
"Father, You already know."
A pause.
A tear.
Then another whisper.
"But I'm coming to You anyway."
No thunder from heaven.
No visible angel.
No immediate miracle.
Just a weary soul approaching God through Jesus Christ.
And that is not a meaningless moment.
That is faith expressing dependence upon the One who is worthy of trust.
Maybe tomorrow the circumstances will change.
Maybe they won't.
Maybe the answer will come sooner than expected.
Maybe the waiting will continue.
But the believer's confidence rests in something more secure than a desired outcome.
It rests in the crucified and risen Savior.
So tonight, when you don't know what to say, pray anyway.
When you are grateful, pray.
When you are convicted of sin, repent and pray.
When you are afraid, pray.
When you are waiting, pray.
When you have no strength left to impress anyone, remember that God never asked you to impress Him.
Jesus has made a way for sinners to come to the Father.
Come through Him.
And remember this whenever the silence feels unbearable:
The Father knew your need before you whispered a word, but through Jesus, He still welcomes you to come close.
